'''Juliet Lee-Franzini''' (1933 &ndash; 2014)<ref name="Juliet Lee-Franzini died January 19, 2014">{{cite web|last1=Grannis|first1=Paul|title=Juliet Lee-Franzini died January 19, 2014|url=http://www-d0.fnal.gov/atwork/memorial/lee-franzini/JulietLee-Franzini.htm|website=www-d0.fnal.gov/|access-date=14 May 2015}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026}}</ref> was a doctor and researcher in [[particle physics]] who founded the [[high energy physics]] experimental group at [[Stony Brook University]].

==Early life and education==
'''Juliet Lee''' was born of Chinese parents in [[Paris, France]] on May 18, 1933<ref name=sciencephoto.com>{{cite web|title=Juliet Lee-Franzini, particle physicist|url=http://www.sciencephoto.com/media/573973/view|website=sciencephoto.com|access-date=14 May 2015}}{{Dead link|date=May 2026}}</ref> and lived her early days on a French farm.

In 1937, at the start of the [[Second Sino-Japanese War|second Sino-Japanese war]], her father was summoned to a diplomatic posting in Hanoi, Vietnam. Her family stayed in Hanoi until 1940, when they moved to Chonqing, China. Juliet attended school sporadically and learned the local Chinese tongue.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=Out of the shadows: contributions of twentieth-century women to physics |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-16962-2 |editor-last=Byers |editor-first=Nina |edition=1. publ., Repr |location=Cambridge |editor-last2=Williams |editor-first2=Gary A.}}</ref>

In 1947, Juliet and her parents moved to New York, where she attended public school and completed the liberal arts curriculum. She also danced ballet and tutored local students in algebra.<ref name=":0" />

After her father acquired a restaurant near [[Columbia University]], Juliet started to drop in on graduate physics classes, which furthered her interest in mathematics.

She earned her BA at [[Hunter College]] in 1953, her MA and PhD from [[Columbia University]] in 1957 and 1960.<ref name="CWP Library UCLA">{{cite web|title=Juliet Lee-Franzini|url=http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Lee-Franzini,_Juliet@901234567.html|website=CWP Library UCLA|access-date=14 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141016131451/http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Lee-Franzini,_Juliet@901234567.html|archive-date=16 October 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> During her education at Columbia, Juliet became interested in the parity violation research.

==Career==

Lee-Franzini first worked as a multilingual guide at the [[United Nations]], then as a cook and waitress at the restaurant at her father's restaurant.<ref name=":0" />

From 1960 to 1962, Juliet worked as a research associate at [[Nevis Laboratories]], at Columbia University. From 1962 to 1963, she became a fellow on the National Academy of Science-National Research Council. In 1963, worked as a professor of physics at [[Stony Brook University|Stony Brook]] and played a leading role in making the lab known for particle physics.<ref name=":0" />

During her Stony Brook tenure, Juliet also served as visiting professor of physics at [[Cornell University]] from 1980 to 1981.

In 1991, she took the position of VIP physicist at the [[Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati]] dell’INFN until 1996, when she became the director of research.<ref name="CWP Library UCLA" /> There, she worked on the [[KLOE (experiment)|KLOE]] research project, which relied on the [[DAFNE|DAFNE electron-positron collider]] to research the matter-antimatter imbalance.<ref>{{Cite journal  |last1=Hellemans |first1=Alexander |title=Italy's KLOE Sets Sights on CP Violation |journal=Science |date=1999 |volume=284 |issue=5414 |pages=568–569 |doi=10.1126/science.284.5414.568b}}</ref>

==Professional board memberships==

Lee-Franzini served on the Board of Directors of The Research Foundation of the [[State University of New York]], from 1986 to 1991. She was on the executive committee of the Division of Particles and Fields at the [[American Physical Society]] from 1987 to 1989. From 1989 to 1991, she was on the nominating committee of the American Physical Society and served on the nominating committee of the Division of Particles and Fields.<ref name="CWP Library UCLA" />

==Research==

Lee-Franzini conducted research at many laboratories over her lifetime. Her experiments in particle physics were conducted at [[Nevis Laboratories|Nevis Labs]], [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], Penn-Princeton Accelerator, [[Fermilab]], [[Cornell University|Cornell]], and [[Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati|Frascati]].

Her early experiments at [[Columbia University|Columbia]] investigated the quantities of [[Muon decay|muon decay spectra]] and revealed accurate confirmation of the V-A nature of the weak interactive force.<ref name="Juliet Lee-Franzini died January 19, 2014" />  She also studied the spectroscopy of bound state [[mesons]], [[quark]] heavy flavor potentials, and the [[KLOE (experiment)|KLOE]] experiments at Frascati.<ref name=sciencephoto.com />

Lee-Franzini and her team used the [[IBM 7090]] at Columbia University to discover the [[CP violation|violation of charge-conjugation invariance in interactions of intermediate strength]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IBM 7090 |url=https://www.columbia.edu/cu/computinghistory/7090.html |access-date=2026-05-03 |website=www.columbia.edu}}</ref> in 1964.

=== Published works ===

* ''Hidden and Open Beauty in CUSB''<ref>{{Citation |last=Lee-Franzini |first=Juliet |date=1998 |title=Hidden and Open Beauty in CUSB |journal=Twenty Beautiful Years of Bottom Physics |series=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=424 |pages=85–96 |doi=10.1063/1.55115 |arxiv=hep-ex/9709025 |bibcode=1998AIPC..424...85L }}</ref>
* ''CP and CPT Studies with Kaons''<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Lee-Franzini |first=Juliet |title=CP and CPT Studies with Kaons |date=2002-09-18 |eprint=hep-ex/0209042}}</ref>
* ''Measurement of &sigma;(e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> &rarr; &pi;<sup>+</sup>&pi;<sup>−</sup>) at e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> colliders''<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Lee-Franzini |first=Juliet |title=Measurement of &sigma;(e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> &rarr; &pi;<sup>+</sup>&pi;<sup>−</sup>) at e<sup>+</sup>e<sup>−</sup> colliders |date=2004-03-02 |eprint=hep-ex/0403006}}</ref>
* ''CP Violation in the K-System'' (1997)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee-Franzini |first1=Juliet |last2=Franzini |first2=Paolo |date=1998-11-01 |title=CP Violation in the K-System |journal=Surveys in High Energy Physics |volume=13 |issue=1–3 |pages=1–44 |doi=10.1080/01422419808240871 |arxiv=hep-ex/9709007 |bibcode=1998SHEP...13....1L |issn=0142-2413}}</ref>

Lee-Franzini was also cited as a collaborator in 32 other research papers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Search {{!}} arXiv e-print repository |url=https://arxiv.org/search/hep-ex?searchtype=author&query=Lee-Franzini,+J |access-date=2026-05-03 |website=arxiv.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Honors==

Juliet Lee-Franzini was recognized as a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref>{{Citation |title=List of fellows of the American Physical Society (1972–1997) |date=2026-03-29 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_fellows_of_the_American_Physical_Society_(1972%E2%80%931997)&oldid=1346066183 |access-date=2026-05-03 |language=en}}</ref> in 1984.

==Personal life==

In 1964, Juliet married fellow physicist Paolo Franzini<ref name=sciencephoto.com /> and took the name Lee-Franzini. They continued to collaborate together professionally throughout their careers.

Juliet gave birth to her daughter Paula in 1965<ref name="CWP Library UCLA" /> in New York. Paula became a physicist, earned a PhD from Stanford in 1987, and published over 30 papers. She changed paths in the 2000s and became a printmaker and painter. She studied visual arts at Ar.Co (Centro de Arte e Comunicação Visual) in Lisbon, Portugal and the [[Saidye Bronfman Centre for the Arts|Saidye Bronfman Center for the Arts]] in Montreal, Canada.

Paula dedicated an art exhibition named ''Fil de Pensée'' to her mother in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EXPOSITIONS 2017 {{!}} Voix Visuelle |url=https://voixvisuelle.ca/fr/expositions-2017/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260504000240/https://voixvisuelle.ca/fr/expositions-2017/ |archive-date=2026-05-04 |access-date=2026-05-04 |website=voixvisuelle.ca |language=fr-FR}}</ref>
